title: Yosemite Needs Your Help Tracking River Otters
summary:
Yosemite National Park is famous for El Capitan, glowing waterfalls, and Half Dome. Now add river otters to the list. The playful mammals have been spotted in the park in Northern California, and rangers want the public's help keeping track of them.

That is harder than it sounds. North American river otters are tricky to monitor, even for experienced rangers and biologists. They have a very high metabolism and can eat about 15 to 20 percent of their body weight in a single day. Much of their time goes to hunting fish, crayfish, crabs, frogs, birds' eggs, and even turtles.

They are also always on the move. One otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams. Yosemite itself has over 1,700 miles of streams, so that is a lot of wet ground to cover. Across Northern California, otters range from Oregon to San Francisco Bay and through the Sierra Nevada mountains.

So rangers are asking visitors to help. If you spot a river otter in Yosemite, note the location, date, and time. Written sightings can be reported in the comments of the park's Facebook post or through the park's contact form. Photos or videos can be shared by direct message on Instagram. 'Your observations can help us better understand how otters roam and use Yosemite's waterways,' the rangers write.

River otters are not endangered, but their history has been rocky. During the 19th and 20th centuries, they were hunted and trapped extensively for their fur, and many were removed from their natural range. Decades of conservation and reintroduction efforts are now helping populations recover. California's population is considered fairly stable, but otters are still at risk from habitat destruction and water pollution.
why_it_matters: Tracking otters helps rangers protect Yosemite's waterways, and healthy otter populations show that rivers and the animals that depend on them are recovering.

background_read: Yosemite is a large national park in Northern California, known for its cliffs, waterfalls and many miles of rivers and streams.
River otters are playful mammals that live in and around water, hunting fish and other small animals.
Rangers and biologists keep track of wildlife in the park, but otters move fast and cover large areas, which makes them hard to follow.
When visitors share sightings, rangers can learn more about where otters roam and how they use the park's waterways.
